newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Lead seen firm, copper to range - trade.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Lead seen firm, copper to range - trade.

text.p: Lead prices will probably hold firm on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on the back of steady buying from China and the Far East while copper may range-trade, base metal dealers said on Friday.
Lead broke through resistance to end at US$700 a tonne on the LME on Thursday, up $21 from the previous day.
"There is the belief that lead will go up. Sentiment is relatively positive," the director of a European metal trading company in the city-state said.
"Lead is looking good," another dealer said.
Steady demand in the Far East, coupled with an uptick in demand in industrialised countries going into winter, underpinned lead's surge, traders said.
"All of a sudden, lead shot up," Vinod Kumar, director of Singapore-based metal company Donald Mcarthy, said.
Most base metal dealers here feel that lead may rise in the short-term by $20-$30.
"But I would think it (lead) will go up more than that," one trader said.
Copper prices, on the other hand, will be looking for leads this afternoon, mainly from the LME stocks report due out at 0900 GMT.
Singapore traders said stocks should go up by about 4,000 to 5,000 tonnes although Kumar predicted a more modest rise of 2,000-3,000 tonnes.
Dealers said the report is likely to be seen by Singapore-based traders as neutral and that the red metal will probably range-trade over the next few days.
"I think it will remain around these levels," Kumar said, adding that three-month copper should see strong support at $2,100 a tonne and resistance at $2,180 a tonne.
But another trader said an increase of 4,000 tonnes may be greeted by the market with yawns.
"The market barely reacted when it went up by 5,000 tonnes last time. Why should it react now?" the trader said. "It's going to probably be dead."
Three month copper prices were seen at around $2,140/45 a tonne at 0430 GMT against the late trade in London yesterday of $2,148 tonne, traders said.
Copper continued to arrive in Singapore warehouses, but the amount involved has declined, traders said.
Some 2,000 tonnes were brought here in the past week and an additional 3,000 tonnes will arrive next week. Most of the material is believed to have come from China.
"Only small amounts are coming to Singapore. They're usually in lots of 500 or 1,000 tonnes," one dealer said.
Traders estimate that at least 20,000 tonnes have not yet been placed on warrant in the LME's Singapore warehouse.
"It's quite a lot," Kumar said when asked about how much copper was stored outside the LME warehouse in the city-state.
Base metal premiums in Singapore continued to remain soft because of the presence of ample material here.
"The presence of that much material here will keep premiums down," one dealer said.
